claims.text: A lightweight HEA based primarily on low-density elements can possess a homogeneous single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
A minor segregation-promoting addition, tuned through solute-size mismatch, can induce controlled nanoscale phase separation.
Such a minor addition can induce nanoscale heterogeneity without significantly increasing alloy density.
Nanoscale chemical fluctuations can pin dislocations and enhance strength in a low-density alloy.
Nanoscale precipitates produced by the addition provide precipitation strengthening.
Nanoscale precipitates and chemical fluctuations act as nucleation sites for protective oxide scales.
Local enrichment of beneficial elements promotes formation of a thin, adherent, protective oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.
Controlled nanoscale heterogeneity improves mechanical strength while preserving ductility.
Controlled nanoscale heterogeneity improves corrosion resistance.
The modified alloy will have higher yield strength and hardness than the homogeneous baseline.
The modified alloy will maintain ductility while increasing strength.
The modified alloy will have a lower corrosion rate than the homogeneous baseline.
The modified alloy will form a thinner and more adherent oxide scale than the homogeneous baseline.
Excessive macroscopic phase separation or brittle intermetallic formation can diminish ductility.
Elemental segregation can compromise oxidation resistance by hindering formation of a protective oxide layer.
The quantitative relationship between the degree of nanoscale heterogeneity and combined mechanical and environmental performance is not yet established.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both mechanical properties and environmental resistance relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed combined-performance mechanism.
